authoredFrom: `overrides` was ruled out for this lane on a grammar inventory — the JSON grammar has no node type for a redefinition — which is the unsound question this lane has now retracted four times (`imports`, `exports`, `extends`, `calls`, all on corpus evidence). A duplicate key in one object IS a redefinition: RFC 8259 §4 says names SHOULD be unique and that a parser's behaviour on a duplicate is unpredictable, and every mainstream parser keeps the LAST one, so the second declaration replaces the first. Measured: 21 NAMED duplicate keys across 11 of 11,713 admitted files, against 120,174 occurrences of the same key in two DIFFERENT objects — which is not a redefinition and is pinned NOT to produce an edge by its companion fixture. The edge shape is the bash lane's, because both declarations share one name and one qualified path: source is the owner symbol, target the key, and `overridesLine` carries the prior line. The `meta.overridesLine` pin is what makes this fixture able to fail a mutant that emits the edge with the wrong prior line — a label-only assertion could not. `contains` endpoints are QUALIFIED PATHS: this pin set was migrated from bare-name endpoints by a structure-preserving transformation (owner and child and line unchanged, spelling resolved against the fixture's own qualifiedName). The reason is measured, not stylistic: over a 202-file, 99-repo sample 32,660 of 66,032 `contains` edges (49.4%) named a target matching MORE THAN ONE published symbol, and the shared resolver declines a non-unique bare name, so those edges bound to no declaration at all. See meta.endpoints=qualified_path on the edge.
